utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday. I would like to greet General Petkovic, I'd like to greet the accused, Defence counsel, Mr. Scott and his associates. I would also like to greet my colleagues, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. Today we shall continue the Praljak cross-examination. The Praljak Defence has given us two binders, and I believe that it is General Praljak who is going to put the questions, himself. Or is it Mr. Kovacic first? Mr. Kovacic, who's starting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good day to everyone. We have decided that, as previously stated in our position, General Praljak will take up all the time that has been allocated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. Good day, General Petkovic. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There are some remarks from colleagues that too many microphones are connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you spoke about the fact that in 1992, you promised that the HVO would assist ABiH, after discussions with Mr. Izetbegovic, with regard to the operation for the liberation of Sarajevo. Please, apart from what you mentioned, were there any other -- was there any other military equipment that you gave to the ABiH, other artillery, and what else did you provide them with?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a T-34 tank was given to them. A 130-millimetre gun and a 122-millimetre howitzer was also directed provided to the ABiH. And everything that was in the Herceg Stjepan Brigade was re-subordinated to them. They re-subordinated the artillery to the command that was in charge of the deblocking of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, was that your personal artillery or did you provide that in agreement with the supreme commander of the HVO and other political bodies within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, naturally that was my -- not my personal equipment. It belonged to the HVO. It couldn't be provided without seeking leave from the highest level of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, were the tank and the howitzer returned to you subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, neither the tank nor the 130-millimetre cannon were returned. They called it Sultan, the Sultan, in fact, and later used it to open fire on us as events unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the tank subsequently used against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was used in the territory of the Konjic municipality. It wasn't returned to the HVO, and as a result it was used against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document 3D03796, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any documents before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Document 3D03796. It's Matiez Frangiz's [phoen] book. He's a Slovenian. It's about arms trafficking that was taking place in Slovenia or through Slovenia, and these were weapons going to Croatia and to the ABiH -- and to Slovenia. Did you have that book?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please have a look at a passage from that book. Have a look at page 72. Have a look at the Croatian text, where reference is made to the 18th of August, 1992, to that date. It has to do with the agreement between Fikret Abdic and Janez Jansa, the minister of defence of the Republic of Slovenia. It is about the agreement to obtain and buy weapons, and so on and so forth. Are you familiar with the fact that this is when this started, and it continued throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the fact that weapons were obtained through Slovenia. Janez Jansa at the time was the minister of defence, I believe, and the main person in Bosnia-Herzegovina was Hasan Cengic, together with his assistants, but Hasan Cengic is the name I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at page 88, where Hasan Cengic is referred to. And how weapons were stored in Brnik is discussed, and how it went missing later, and it was a huge incident in Slovenia. Are you familiar with this? Did you learn about this later?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a subject discussed in Slovenia. The weapons arrived in Koper and then they disappeared, probably transported to Bosnia by plane, helicopter. First taken to Brnik, I assume, and then transported further on to Bosnia. Brnik is an airport in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please look at 112, where reference is made to the fact that weapons had to be transported in humanitarian convoys, the Children of Europe Fund convoys. It also refers to where the weapons came from, how it landed in Budapest without the Hungarian authorities being aware of the fact, and then this equipment arrived in Slovenia. The intention was that it should then be transported to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Money is also referred to, and Al-Fatiq Al-Hussein [phoen], a director is mentioned. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Children of Europe Fund is concerned, I've heard about that. But the weapons were obtained in that manner at the time, yes, that's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at page 130 and 131 in the Croatian text. Reference is made to the amounts of money paid for equipment. So 520 soldiers of the ABiH, for Bosnia soldiers, who arrived in Slovenia from Western European countries, they were equipped there and were sent in two groups in the direction of Bosnia and Herzegovina via Croatia. And a reference is made to how much that cost. My question is as follows: Are you aware of the fact that there were groups -- volunteer groups from Western Europe, volunteer Muslims, who went through Croatia and Slovenia, they were equipped and trained there, and they went from Slovenia, through Croatia, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from the HZ-HB -- what is called the HZ-HB, they would enter Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were equipped and trained members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that was the usual route, but they weren't as well equipped in Slovenia as they were in Croatia. Things were done much more freely in Croatia than in Slovenia. But such things occurred in Slovenia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 365, there's a list of names. Have a look at the name "Hasan Cengic." How many times is this person referred to as someone who is involved with arms? What do you know about Hasan Cengic, and what sort of a role did he play in the ABiH? Whose money did he use to buy weapons with?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard that Hasan Cengic represented the ABiH government. He was the main person who would receive money, and in Croatia and the surrounding countries he would reach agreements about purchasing weapons. So he was the person through whom all these things were done. He was a pivotal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. Before we continue, good afternoon, Your Honours, and all those in and around the courtroom. Just for the Prosecution to continue making its record on this point, and I won't do it in every instance, to spare everyone in the courtroom from that, but I want to make a record that this is yet again another new topic. There was nothing about this or Mr. Cengic in any of the examinations to date, so it's once again the type of new material, new topic, that the Prosecution's noted before, and I want to make that clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. As far as I remember, the issue of armament requirement was mentioned in direct. Hasan Cengic, as one who participated in this huge job, was not, that is true, but the issue was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just want to make clear I don't consider -- you can boil this down to such a general level, you can say that this whole subject of armaments provided during the war, over a three- or four year period, and that subject covers everything. I think that's not fair or reasonable. You can't just continue on and on about a subject because somebody mentioned it in some passing way and going into a whole different area of it, so I think that's only fair. Otherwise, the rule is meaningless.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I'll start again. On behalf of the Petkovic Defence, we'd just like to make our record that we don't understand and we suggest there's no basis on which what Mr. Scott says constitutes any objection at all. Expiration of these matters are well within the ambit of cross-examination, as has been made absolutely clear on a number of rulings by the Trial Chamber. It follows that since there is no valid basis for an objection, there is really no valid basis for any comment at all as we go along in the course of cross-examination of this witness by this particular accused. Mr. Scott's made his record, but it wasn't appropriate and really ought to be disregarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in that case, let me make it again. It is my objection. My objection is to apply the rules of this Chamber, which provides that when a co-accused goes into new materials and new topics on an examination, it has to be treated as direct examination and there shall be no leading questions. The time should be charged against some bank of time used for that -- by that party for their examinations-in-chief. So this examination being conducted now by Mr. Praljak must be charged against some time that I suppose the Praljak Defence still has left, and the Prosecution must be given equal amount of time to cross-examine as the effect of direct examination. So those are the rules and the guide-lines of the Chamber. I ask that they be applied, and I do make my record on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's an entirely different point -- those are entirely different points which I don't propose to trouble the Trial Chamber and take your time on that. It's maybe a battle we will specifically fight when it specifically affects our cross-examination of a witness in relation to other accused. But those are different points. The first record-making that Mr. Scott made this afternoon or purported to make had nothing to do with those points. If he wants to object to a leading question, for example, he should object to a leading question, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall read the guide-line of the 24th of April, 2008, which settles the issue. Page 4, paragraph 8, I shall read it out slowly: "However, the cross-examination relating to an issue which has not been mentioned during examination-in-chief is not a cross-examination, per se, but an examination as is examination-in-chief." Therefore, the rules that apply for the latter must be abided by. Consequently, leading questions would not be allowed, when these type of questions are being put. General Praljak, do not put your question in a leading manner, but address them in a neutral fashion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- before Mr. Praljak proceeds, I want to recall some of the cross-examination that I conducted last Thursday. You may recall on the one of the videos I asked the specific question, with respect to a question asked of Dr. Prlic, on foreign credits that the Sarajevo government was rumoured to be seeking for armament purposes. It would seem to me that this line of questioning is in direct connection with that. You know, we're talking about a very fluid event, so the issue has been raised. And, therefore, I just wish to put that on the record and remind everybody. And I understand the Prosecution's position. I think at some point the Prosecution, as it has already, will be demanding additional time because of these topics, and I think that's an issue that can be addressed later on. But for these purposes, I think this issue has been raised, and in my respectful submission, General Praljak should be allowed to conduct cross-examination as opposed to direct examination with time being taken away from some of his allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I only have two sentences. I consider the essence of Mr. Scott's objection being the request for additional time to examine Mr. Petkovic. There is no rule, however, no one paragraph in the guide-lines or in any case law of this Tribunal, which would allow for the Prosecution's time for cross-examination to depend on the time spent by other Defences. If Rule 90(H)(1) allows addressing new topics in cross-examination, and if the Trial Chamber, in its explicit decision, allowed the Prosecutor to -- even to cross-examine the Defence witnesses even after the Prosecution case, and raise or deal with new topics, I believe that the objection that -- or, rather, the request to allow for additional time for the Prosecution on this basis is totally unfounded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, my final question, and it is not leading. How and through which country or which organisation was the ABiH able to arm itself, and how did it arm all the 250.000 men that Sefer Halilovic claims they had in their ranks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't want to go into the issue of sources, but it had to arrive through Croatia. There was no other way. So all this materiel arrived in Croatia and went through the Herceg-Bosna area to the ABiH, and part of it arrived through Cengic to Croatia, from where it was transported to the ABiH in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The question -- the following question was raised already, and you answered it, General. It has to do with volunteers in the HVO and the ABiH, Croatia, et cetera. So here's my question to you: I brought a document about it. How many citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were volunteers in the Croatian Army in 1991 and in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that number is anywhere between 10.000 to 13.000 soldiers. And let me add, in October 1993 there is information on record that about 10.000 remained in the Croatian Army at that time, and they were Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And do you draw the conclusion from that that Bosnia-Herzegovina was involved in the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina went to the theatre of war in Croatia. They joined the Croatian Army and fought the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You answered Judge Antonetti's question about your having a telephone in your vehicle. What kind of telephone was that, and from where was it possible to make a phone call or engage in a phone conversation, and who, apart from you, had such a phone in their vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards the army, I'm the only one who had such a phone. None of my commanders at any level had one. There were four or five at other levels, however, outside the army. They were the earliest Benefons, as they were called, but you couldn't make calls everywhere. Once you left Mostar and reached Siroki Brijeg and continued to Grude, you may be -- you may have been available for a certain time. The best connectivity was possible if you were in Croatia, and you could receive phone calls from Croatia. However, the postal network in Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't function well. That's why many people simply left those phones in their cars and didn't rely on them much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, tell us, what is the highest decoration in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and it's been mentioned today -- these days, rather, it's the Golden Lily. There are some protesters mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, General Praljak has changed his line of questions. I would like to get back to something. When I put a question, it is because it is relevant, in light of the indictment. I don't waste my time putting questions of no interest. And if someone feels it is irrelevant, I should be told immediately. Why is this business about the telephone relevant? It is relevant in light of Article 7(3) of the Statute, i.e., your responsibility during a particular period. The Appeals Chamber is extremely vigilant in this regard. It feels that a commander should exercise control, and that when there is no control over the events, this means that he is not incriminated. This was the case of Dragomir Milosevic. When I put the question to you on the question of the telephone, is that I had this at the back of my mind. I always have things at the back of my mind, two essential questions, what relates to fact and what relates to the law. As far as the fact was concerned, I wanted to know how your telephone operates. And when it comes to the law, it has to do, at the back of my mind, with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. And those two questions are always at the back of my mind. You said that General Praljak came back, but I am totally lost. You said that you were the only person having this telephone. Fine. But when you were in Split, did the telephone network enable you, via this telephone, to contact your officers who had remained in Mostar, or were you no longer in contact? At the same time as you, I had a Motorola, which was a very similar telephone. But when I changed area, the coverage wasn't the same, and sometimes there was a complete void and I couldn't contact anyone. When you were in Split, was it possible to reach you over this phone? This is a very technical question, but behind this question there is the essential issue of Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the phone exchanges in Bosnia-Herzegovina, once the repeater stations were destroyed in that republic, the exchanges were -- could function only in the closest proximity. It was necessary for you, to receive a call from Croatia, for somebody to be able to reach you through a repeater somewhere else. But these phones were very unreliable, because otherwise they would have been used in more vehicles. I used two vehicles, one offered vehicle and one personal car -- passenger car, rather, but I never took my phone from one car to another because the function wasn't really -- the functioning wasn't good. All Bosnian phone exchanges could only serve the needs of the local area, because the repeater stations had been destroyed by the JNA, the one on Mount Velez and elsewhere too. I believe that we've heard somebody speaking about that here. And that was the problem with regard to that phone, so it was more of a decoration than a practical tool. For a hundred metres or so there was coverage, and then for kilometres there would be no coverage, so the phone was more or less useless. And that's why they stopped procuring these phones and giving it to other command structures, because it proved inefficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you said. Do you remember, General, while I was commander, did I ever have such a phone, for the very reason that given an area of 10 square kilometres, you may be able to use it only at two or three spots, so it was a totally unreliable means of communication?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The vehicle that had this in-built telephone was eventually given to the Logistics Base at Grude, because once you set off for Rama or Tomislavgrad, you weren't able to use it anywhere else. And you know well that you received another off-road vehicle which I had used before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I haven't finished with the question about the Golden Lily. Did you -- were you awarded that highest decoration of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of October, Ejub Ganic, in the presence of Stjepan Kljujic and Stjepan Siber and three or four officers of the ABiH, awarded me the Golden Lily. That was in 1992, in the building of the -- sorry, in the building of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, you replied to Judge Antonetti's question about whether or not Sefer Halilovic could have been or could not have been or was or wasn't a man who, in the JNA, was a high-ranking KOS officer, so please take a look at 3D3023.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it in the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the second binder. There are two. You got two binders. This is in the second one. And, Usher, if you would be so kind as to give the second binder too. It is the last document in that binder. [Interpretation] It's the last document in the second binder. Yes, the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are three tabs, but without any numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What you see is the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. It's a document dated 24 May 1993, and it clearly says that Sefer Halilovic was an agent of the Military Intelligence Service, he had the pseudonym "Boris," and this is a summary of the relevant information. It also mentions that since 9 February 1977, he was an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not familiar with this document, and that's why I replied that I didn't have that information. I was in the HVO then and contacted with Halilovic, so I could have used that information, but unfortunately I never received it. However, given the fact that I haven't read it, I cannot comment. Now I can see here that this issue is extensively dealt with here, but you know my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Under number 2 of the same document, you see a monthly plan of activity, after which you can see personal information. It's a JNA document and says that Sefer Halilovic, son of Rustem, was an officer, a Muslim, and a collaborator of the security services, and so on. The most important thing, however, are these minutes. So here's my question: Do you know that on the 5th of November, 1993, the MUP in Sarajevo, the State Security Service, to be more precise, questioned Mr. Sefer Halilovic and that he gave a long interview in which he ambiguously admits that he was a KOS officer? He also says what he did. And at the end of that document, we can see both Halilovic's signature and the signature of the one who interviewed him. Did you know that Sefer Halilovic was questioned, once he was replaced, and that he gave such a statement? Unfortunately, I cannot translate all this or have it all translated, but it follows unambiguously from all this that he was, indeed, a KOS officer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see in this document that it was compiled on the 5th of November, 1993, and that Sefer Halilovic signed or initialled every page of this statement. This is a document that his own security centre in Sarajevo made. They interviewed him and took a statement, but I have never had this statement on my hands before. This is that same problem again with regard to what I do or don't know about Sefer Halilovic. I can see that this document was made on the 5th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now go into something that was dealt with in the examination-in-chief, and that was the use of the Croatian Army in the south, along the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So please take a look at the map, 3D3163. It's in the back.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Praljak, Your Honours, I know this map. This map was produced in the command of the 4th Army District, whose commander I was at the time. It bears the signature of my deputy, Mr. Petkovic, and there's also my -- our military post office number. It was made as a part of the effort to reconstruct wartime events in the Republic of Croatia. So I was charged to do that with the south of Croatia, as I was a commander there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, please draw on this map the directions along which the JNA attacked the south of Croatia, the directions of their advance.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will mark the direction that cuts through -- or, rather, that goes along the territory of Croatia and the directions that cut through the territory, as well as the maritime blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, please mark, and mark these directions and put the figures 1, 2, 3, next to them. Your Honours, I sat down so I can see, so I hope you won't mind. And please be clear what time-period this is.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the 8th of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please draw the axis of attack.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the Republic of Croatia, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, on the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Number 1. This is under number 1, the taking of Konovlje [phoen]. This is the first stage. This image is not very clear. Can you enlarge it so I can see Dubrovnik, so that I can exclude this area? I'm really trying hard here, but with these glasses --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Further up at the highest point, can you see Rijeka Dubrovacka?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and continue. Above Dubrovnik, there is the second stage, the breakthrough through Croatia [marks]. And as far as I can see here, as far as I can see Dubrovnik, the town of Dubrovnik here --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, have a look at the Rijeka Dubrovacka. Whose control was Rijeka Dubrovacka?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rijeka Dubrovacka and then the urban settlement -- the suburban settlement of Mokosica was under the control of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you mark this with number 3?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I use my finger? How can you erase this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Leave that there. Cross out number 3 and then mark the area around the town itself, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, it is seen that you can draw across -- you can cancel what you have written. Can you delete what you have written? And you can reposition yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be best if -- well, that's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Below Rijeka Dubrovacka?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see Dubrovnik up there, but it's very difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the town of Dubrovnik that was under a blockade. The Army of Yugoslavia never managed to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Your Honours, this is the direction through the Republic of Croatia. After that direction, there were attacks from the flank from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that with number 4, please, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Do you want me to draw the line to the point that was reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you help me? Is this the Bay of Ston? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that with number 5, please. Is that the point that was reached by the forces of the JNA? Did they take that territory?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA was stopped there, and the Croatian Army, in May 1992, launched a counter-attack to liberate the south of Croatia from the that point: I can also mark this [marks], the movement of JNA ships. It was a naval blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark that with number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you correct number 5, please, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this could be erased, please, because I think that the tip of the pen doesn't actually trace the line that I try to draw. Who assisted me a while ago and erased number 5? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I crossed out -- I erased number 5, the old number 5, and I've marked it with "5" again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you mark this area with number 6, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here [marks]?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what is this? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This represents the ships of the JNA Navy. They were in the vicinity of Dubrovnik, and they were maintaining a naval blockade. They prevented humanitarian ships from reaching the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, in your opinion -- well, please, tell me, apart from number 5, which remained free, were all the other areas occupied by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the occupied territory of Southern Croatia, with the exception of the town of Dubrovnik. The town, itself, was not actually occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at the following document, 3D3800. And before we do that -- and just a minute, please. Could we have an IC number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, could we have a number for that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just marked by the witness, which is 3D03163, shall be given Exhibit IC01190. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I have a follow-up question: We've just had a look at the document, and with the blue lines you've indicated the attack direction by JNA, and you've given the date of 15 May 1992 for Dubrovnik. I've listened to you, and I would like to know how relevant this is for the indictment. General Petkovic, I would like to know why you consider that this is relevant for us to understand what you are charged with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction. I mentioned May 1992 as the date when the Croatian Army launched a counter-attack and repulsed the JNA. The attack on the south of the Republic of Croatia commenced -- well, I think it was on the 8th or the 10th of October, 1991. That is when this attack was launched on the Republic of Croatia. This is important because the Republic of Croatia, in order to defend this narrow part of its territory and to subsequently liberate it, had to go into a certain depth beyond the border of the Republic of Croatia. It had to enter the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So Croatia wasn't able to resist this act of aggression by maintaining its units in its own territory. It had to defend itself and attack the flank forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It had to wait in the border area, but on the Bosnia-Herzegovina side of the border. So in some cases the Croatian Army had to penetrate to a depth of 500 metres or 1 kilometre in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to put an end to the flank attacks launched by the JNA against the Republic of Croatia, because the JNA used the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina quite freely; and as a result, the Croatia Army had to take up the most appropriate positions available at the time. And later on, the Croatian Army, whenever possible, kept to its borders, once this southern part had been liberated, stayed within its borders, but there were certain areas; for example, the area of Popovo Polje, where the Army of Croatia had to enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sometimes it had to go to a distance of 300 metres, sometimes 500 metres, sometimes 700 metres. It wasn't possible to do this otherwise. The members of the Bosnian Serb Army took advantage of this later. You showed me a document from November 1992 which shows that I had discussions with Mladic. It was November 1992. I think it was the 29th, something like that. And General Mladic requested at meeting of -- he wanted to speak about these forces in the border area towards the south of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, General Petkovic: You are not a legal expert, but you are the chief of staff of HVO and you are a commander in the Croatian Army. You might have a military answer, and this is relevant, and this concerns the indictment. When you go into a foreign territory about one kilometre deep, in your eyes do you consider that this is an armed -- an international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that wouldn't be an example of an international armed conflict. It was a matter of necessity, in tactical and operative terms. It was necessary to resist the forces that didn't want to put an end to their attack. I should also mention the fact that after these events, you know that in July an agreement on friendship and co-operation was signed between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, mentioned border co-operation between the two armies. Mr. Izetbegovic also thought that this was an attack -- if Mr. Izetbegovic had thought that this was an attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina, he wouldn't have signed an agreement with Croatia, and he wouldn't have said that the army would co-operate in this border area or this cross-border area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Are you aware of the jurisprudence of the Russian Constitutional Court on an international conflict concerning the intervention of the Russian Army in Chechnya? In Chechnya, not Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I wasn't familiar with this. All I knew was the situation of the JNA, and we had the right to drive back the enemy and set up defence positions in the most appropriate places. That didn't mean we had to occupy the territory. But with regard to the border, we had to take up positions at points that were closest to the border. In other words, we had to take up positions in the tactical depth, the so-called tactical depth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, tell me, which was the furthest line that the Croatian Army, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had its positions which was the most distant line that it had its positions at?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the part in the south of Croatia. It's TG-2. It's to the west -- or, rather, the south-west of the Bregava River. I think the river is called the Bregava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Where is it from Stolac?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It goes from Stolac to Capljina and Svitava. It flows from Stolac. I've already marked the positions here. You can see them. It's three or four kilometres in the depth of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards a feature called Stolovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me two more things. With regard to the liberation of the eastern and western bank of Mostar, the southern part down there too, was the Croatian Army involved in that liberation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Army was responsible for this part in the border-line area. We had the witness Beneta who was here, and it didn't cross the line by the Bregava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now for another question. While the JNA was attacking what you mentioned in 1991, while it was involved in activities in the village of Ravno, the events in Ravno - we've heard about that on numerous occasions here - what did the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, have to state about that, and everyone else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a statement, Your Honours, that was relayed through the media at the time according to which it was said that that was not our war. It's not our war, is what he said. Everyone interpreted this in his own manner, but however was involved in the war took this to mean it's your problem, not mine, in spite of the fact that a war was being waged in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there were these two places in Bosnia-Herzegovina that had been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now for the following document, which is 3D3800. 3D3800. It's a book written by the former president of Croatia, Mr. Stjepan Mesic. What I'm interested in has to do with the question put by Judge Antonetti, a question about whether the JNA had the right to attack Dubrovnik, given that Croatia had not yet been recognised by the European Union, and therefore that might mean that the army was punishing certain renegade bands, groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, you've had this book before you and you've seen this book. It's page 202 in the Croatian version. It's -- the date is the 26th of October, 1991, Saturday. And who was heading in the direction of Dubrovnik at the time or what?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time President Mesic had organised a humanitarian convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He wasn't president at the time, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, please, what was Mr. Mesic's title at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. That's what he was in October when, on a ship called Slavonia I, he set off in the direction of Dubrovnik in order to assist this town and to break up the JNA blockade. He believed that as the supreme commander, if he appeared in that area, he would be able to exercise an influence on the command structure of the JNA and persuade them to cease with the activities that they had started engaging in in the territory of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many boats were escorting the large ship we have referred to; 400, 500, or 600?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few of them. I can't tell you how many exactly. Quite a few people joined -- joined up, decided to escort the ship. There was the common will to put an end to the blockade of Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at page 207 and 208 now, please. It's in the Croatian text. And please tell me what happened to the commander of the JNA or, rather, to the president of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic Of Yugoslavia, as this biographer states in this book, and can you say whether what is stated here is, in fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have read the book. I've had the opportunity to listen to Mr. Mesic, the president of the Republic of Croatia, commenting on the events at that time. The JNA did not listen to him. They even ordered him to change his course for Dubrovnik, that they had to go to the war port of Zelenika which is in the Bay of -- the Boka Kotorska Bay. So there was significant problems. The JNA didn't want to listen to Mr. Mesic, as the president of Yugoslavia, the supreme commander, so there was this intent to take the boat to Montenegro. It was difficult to persuade them to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at what Stipe Mesic says to Brovet. I quote: "You suspect your own commander, your own president, and your supreme commander." I quote Mesic: "Admiral Brovet, do you know what you are doing? You doubt your own president and the supreme commander -- you are suspecting your own president and the supreme command of terrorism." And Brovet answers, I quote: "Leave that alone, Mr. President. Leave that subject for your happy presidential sessions. This is a war. Fire is opened. People are dying. There are no attempts to politically out-smarting others here. There are no tricks." General, were any hostages taken? That's my first question, and my second question is: Is this a kind of military coup? Who is in charge of the state?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a classical military coup, and it happened early. Initially, they tried to prevent Mr. Mesic from becoming the president of the Presidency and to enable the army to take over. But when Mr. Mesic finally managed to take up his position as president of the Presidency, then the Presidency was split, it was four votes against four and the Presidency was in a deadlock. That's the situation the army used to do what they wanted to do. Serbia had its four votes in the Presidency and couldn't get a fifth one, so it was a deadlock, and this was a sign for Brovet, Kadijevic, Adzic and the others that the JNA could proceed the way it thought fit, and they acted accordingly. So that Mesic was the supreme commander on paper only, but he didn't have the support of the Presidency because it was in a deadlock. He needed another vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right, all right. General, let me repeat the question: When the army doesn't obey its supreme commander, but instead searches its ship, what do you call that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I call it a coup d'etat or a military coup.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If you know, who was on board that ship of the French?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kouchner, I believe his name was. I believe that sometime ago he even gave an interview for Croatian Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Let me just correct the transcript right away, because there may be misunderstanding and additional questions. Page 27, line 2, it says "searches its ship," so which can mislead us to conclude that the JNA searched its own ship, but rather it searched the president's ship.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavija was a large passenger ship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but on board that passenger ship there was the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said Mr. Kouchner was a foreign American, a Hungarian or a Swiss person. I don't know. This may not mean much. Mr. Kouchner, who was Mr. Kouchner, who is Mr. Kouchner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what his duty was or his position in the French government. He was a French national and a high-ranking French government official at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is he a minister of foreign affairs of the French Republic today?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot to ask you about the documents about Sefer Halilovic which you weren't familiar with. I'll be as accurate as possible. Is it possible, judging by the documents that we saw, that Sefer Halilovic kept up his contacts with his former principals?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's difficult for me to tell, whether or not he remained in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Please take a look at the following document now, 3D00942. I'll have a short question for you about that, 3D00942. It's a book that we've already seen. It's by Sefko Hodzic, "The Unsealed Envelope," and I'll direct you to page 188, where it says, about the Neretva 93 campaign -- he says: "They were singing songs to Alija, Sefer and Haso," referring -- they -- he refers to the soldiers of the ABiH, and also songs about their native town of Klis. And when they put up their tents and set off for Voljevac to take part in the battle for Crni Vrh on the following day. When they were on the trucks, they started singing. I quote: "Wake up, 'balija.' May God strike you down. We're going to Prozor. Fuck your father." So, General, it is true that "balija" is a derogatory term, but doesn't this show that they sometimes make jokes about this very term? They, I think, call themselves "balija" sometimes. So this may sound leading, but tell us what you think.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that they communicated that way, and I witnessed that in Edo Bajram's pub in Mostar, where both Croats and Muslims would gather, and they communicated in this way. They called -- one called another "balija," but nobody minded. Everybody laughed, et cetera, especially at Edo Bajram's. That's a restaurant in Mostar where I would go sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us now deal with the issue of the Bijela Bridge and the topic of Mostar being under siege. So please go to the following document, because I'll first show you some documents, 3D00567. One of the documents is an exhibit already. Take a look at it and tell us who signed it. And what does the document say, clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document of the Command of the 4th Corps, dated the 23rd of April, 1993. It's an order issued to the 44th Brigade at Jablanica, and it's signed by Arif Pasalic, commander -- or, rather, it says "Arif Pasalic, Commander," but in fact it was signed by Mr. Budakovic. I know his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What does the document say, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the order is to be forwarded to the 4th Battalion of the 41st Brigade, Dreznica, to de-mine the Bijela Bridge. So the 41st Brigade was a part of the -- of a larger Mostar unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who controls the Bijela Bridge at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH, because it says here that nobody can remain on the bridge except for those securing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3D01018. It's dated the 6th of May, 1993. You know Colonel Miljenko Lasic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What happened on Bijela Bridge? Look at item 4, and who controls the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bijela Bridge was still under control of the ABiH. Item 4 deals with an incident that happened when a convoy of the SpaBat was returning from Jablanica, and ABiH members opened fire and wounded three European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 4D00768. You know who Rasim Delic was?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At that time, Rasim Delic was the commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't go so fast. I find it difficult to follow. I'm looking at the document to see whether General Petkovic is changing his views or changing topic. Seemingly, the bridge is not mentioned here anymore, but I'd like to get back to the bridge. As you know, I put questions on the Mostar Bridge several times. My question seemed to me to be very relevant, since the Mostar Bridge is mentioned in the indictment. In this case, we've just heard about the Bijela Bridge, which was mined by the ABiH. On listening to the answer you provided - you were fortunate enough to go to a war school, which is not the case for all and every one - can you tell us, as regards the training an officer gets, is he told that a bridge which is of strategic importance should be mined in case this bridge would fall in the hands of the enemy? Is this something which you are taught at military school or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, that is something that's taught at military schools, but the war plans of the former JNA clearly laid out which bridge would be demolished and in which situation, and each bridge were already prepared for demolishing. Of course, the details were strictly secret, and they were part of the so-called war plans of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you say this, does this mean that the rule could have applied to the Old Bridge or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Old Bridge were to be used for military purposes, yes, absolutely, the rules could have been applied. Any facility or building used for military purposes, irrespective of its nature, is something these rules applied to, because whoever use this building or facility in such a way will bear the full responsibility of any damage done to that facility or building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The document is 4D -- take a look at item 3. It's dated the 27th of July. Just item 3, and be very brief, please. Time is running out. Look at what Rasim Delic is saying, "crossing over from Dobrinja to Butmir and transport from Igman to Mostar," and so on. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that this crossing, and he mentions the direction from Dobrinja to Butmir, that includes the Sarajevo Airport, controlled by UNPROFOR, and "transport" implies transportation of motor vehicles, and the concrete direction here being Igman to Mostar, the first destination being Igman and the final destination Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And transport from Igman to Mostar, what does that mean, something is transported?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means if you have 200 soldiers, you will have to put them on six trucks or something, and you'll establish a column which will move along the direction stated and finally arrive at the destination, which in this case is Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 4D726. The date is the 26th of October. It's the last document in a series. Look at the signature and tell us what is now happening with Bijela Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also an ABiH document produced by its 4th Corps, and Sulejman Budakovic signed for Arif Pasalic. He was his deputy. This says that a line must be strengthened. They are mentioning Kuci, Bijela Creek, and prevent the infiltration of sabotage groups on the left banks in the region of Salakovac, Bijela Creek, and they are requesting that 20 soldiers be sent there to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now look at 3D03789. That's a map; or, rather, a satellite photograph, 3D43-1385. General, tell us, please, very clearly, whether the Bijela Most, until its eventual destruction, into which we can't go now, was usable, and was even the roundabout road usable? And tell us, if the water-level should go down, and who controlled the dams? Was it possible to use the roundabout road even at the time of the fiercest ABiH attacks against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you discharge water from the Salakovac Lake, in the area of Bijela Bridge there was the old bridge [realtime transcript read in error "Old Bridge"] which would be flooded -- or which was flooded, and at that moment it became fully usable, and then it was possible to use the road around this Bijela Bay, if I may call it that, and the Salakovac Dam was controlled by the ABiH, and that's downstream from Bijela Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. I think -- I may be mistaken, Your Honours, but so there is no confusion in the courtroom or in the record, I think the reference here is not the old bridge in Mostar but it's talking about another bridge that used to be near the Bijela on the -- near the Bijela Bridge. If that could be clarified, please. It's in the transcript as an "Old Bridge" capitalised, as if it's in reference to the Stari Most, and I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague is correct. I also wanted to tell that. It is error. "Bijela Bridge" is correct, but "Old Bridge" which is mentioned in line 25 of page 32 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I said "old bridge," I was referring to the bridge that existed before the new one over the Bijela Bay was built, so in that location. There was an old bridge that was in existence before the new one was built. And when the level of the water fell by two and a half or three metres in the Lake of Salakovac, that old bridge would then appear -- re-appear and could then be used to cross from one side to the other. Naturally, it was necessary to carry out repairs on the entrance and exit to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, tell me, who controlled the dams on the Neretva after the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the dams on the River of Neretva after the 30th of June, 1993, were under the control of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd now like to see P011081. It's a map that the Prosecution has shown. P011081 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The usher -- I would kindly ask usher to remove the first one -- the first map which is there. Mr. Praljak called the map which is under.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a map from the Prosecution, a map of the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, of the positions of the ABiH and of the HVO at the time of the conflict in Mostar. That's the second half of the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, please point out the positions of the artillery of the Army of Republika Srpska from Rosci to the south.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're referring to this map. Should I show the positions or mark them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark them. Yes, mark them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite far away, so I won't be able to mark it and speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we place it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Usher, please. I think we have it also in e-court, so it could be on the ELMO and witness could make markings on the screen. It will be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Petkovic, this is a Prosecution map. It shows the artillery positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, of the HVO. Unfortunately, the artillery positions of the ABiH aren't indicated. But, please, when the map does appear, could you show me the positions of the artillery of the Army of Republika Srpska from Rosci, from the north, to the south?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps we should take a break, because obviously there is a technical problem with that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the Registrar has told me. There it is now. Mr. Kovacic, would you like to have a break now, because the map is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, still it would be good to make a break, because it is a block of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to ask for your leave to have contact with our client in the course of this break. It has to do with regard to the Prosecution's response to the request for additional time. We have our response, but we would like to speak to the general and have his agreement for our positions in our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall ask my colleagues if they agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They agree, so you may. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, you have the map before you now. Please use large circles to mark the positions of the artillery of the Army of Republika Srpska from the north, Rosci to the south.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area of the so-called Rosci mountain [marks]. This is number 2 [marks], and, Your Honours, we called this area Zijemlje. It's a fairly large area. Number 3 is the location above Eastern Mostar [marks]. Number 4 is the location that was to the west of Blagaj [marks]. And you can't see an important location in this map, a location which was to the east about four kilometres from Blagaj. I think the name of the place was Cobanovo Polje. You can't see it in this map. In this direction [marks] there is another location that is called Cobanovo Polje. I think it was about four kilometres to the east of Blagaj. That's where the last defence lines of the ABiH were, in this area. So there were four significant locations at which the Army of Republika Srpska had its artillery as well as tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be better to put this map on the ELMO. Could you please place it on the ELMO? Could the usher assist us so that we can see the location I'm interested in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am a little bit confused, because the question was mark the position of the artillery of the -- oh, yes, of the Army of Republika Srpska. I thought it was about the JNA. Mr. Petkovic, where was the JNA artillery? Yes, Republika Srpska-JNA. But then at the end, did you -- I misunderstand something. I'm very sorry. Please regard my words as not spoken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I have understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. This is a Prosecution map. They pointed out that they received it from the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the government. That's the time when, according to the claims made, Mostar was surrounded. That's what it says here. So could we please place this map on the ELMO so that we can move on and deal with other positions at which the Army of Republika Srpska had its artillery. Yes, we haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your map, according to you, you have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. I would like to know the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, this is from the second half of 1993, when there were clashes between the ABiH and the HVO. The Prosecution made this map for that purpose, and they pointed out, although the map has been signed, and I quote -- they said that the map was drawn up by the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a concept that is somewhat too broad, but that's what was stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's -- with reference to what my colleague has said - he was talking about an important legal issue - according to you, this is Republika Srpska or JNA, who's there, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, at that time the JNA had withdrawn by June 1992, so these are the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska. And I would just like to add something else of importance. These are positions that remained as such from the second half of 1992. These positions didn't change almost until the end of the war. These are the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, as far as the Herzegovina Corps is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic -- [overlapping speakers] -- withdrawn in June 1992, but when I ask a question, I always have a legal framework in mind, always, and I'm going to insist on this with all my questions. I asked the question because I wanted to know whether it was the JNA or the Republika Srpska, because the International Court of Justice, which is not very far from us, has, in the decision that was rendered said that JNA had withdrawn in May 1992 and that it was the Army of Republika Srpska that was there. That's why I was asking you to please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar -- would you like to have an IC number or not? You do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think it is misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some other questions for that map, and then I will ask for an IC number. But what we'll now see on the ELMO is the southern area that cannot be seen on the first map, so please have a look at the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at the area that is to the south. It hasn't been marked here. And, General, this is a Google map, and could you please mark the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska on this map and the positions of its artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Your Honours, I can only indicate this location above Mostar here [indicates]. I marked this location on the previous map with number 3. I don't know if General Praljak would like me to mark this location with the very same number, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. And this would be location number 4 [marks], which is identical to the location referred to. Don't ask me to be more precise. Let me see if I can locate Cobanovo Polje to the east of Blagaj. If not, I'll just use an arrow to indicate the direction. This is Blagaj here [indicates]. Cobanovo Polje --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark it with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll mark it like this [marks] and use an arrow pointing in this direction. It was four to five kilometres to the east of Blagaj. That's where the VRS had its artillery, and it's a location that we can't see on the previous mark that was produced by the Prosecution. I'll mark this location with number 5 [marks]. Perhaps it was a kilometre or a kilometre and a half from this point that I have now marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What was the ratio, when it comes to the forces, in the second half of 1993? We can ignore the previous period. What was the ratio of the artillery of the VRS and the HVO artillery in that area? So what was the balance of forces in that area of South-Eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ratio was 8:1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And to whose benefit was that ratio?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the benefit of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Use the very same map to indicate the positions of the VRS, please. Mark it with number 6.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have a red pen, or shall I use the very same blue pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Use the blue pen.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petkovic, do you want me to mark this with number 6 to show that this is the position of the VRS? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, now please sign this map.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map just signed by the witness on the ELMO shall be given Exhibit IC01191. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I'm putting my following question, my next question, could we please -- or before I do so, could we have the next map placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, the map -- the previous map doesn't have an IC number yet, but on the previous map we don't have the positions of the artillery of VRS marked. My question is: Did the ABiH, in fact, have artillery positions, and when, in fact, did the ABiH have its artillery take up positions in that area with regard to the HVO artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH naturally had its artillery in this area. On the whole, they had 120-millimetre mortars. However, they also had 122-millimetre howitzers, and later that number increased when equipment arrived from Jablanica, I think, two or three 122 howitzers arrived from that area. So the relationship -- the ratio between the HVO and the ABiH was 1:2.5 to the benefit of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to correct the transcript. On page 40, line 24, the question seems to have to do with the VRS and its artillery positions, but the general, in fact, said that you couldn't see the artillery positions of the ABiH. And then the question was whether the ABiH had artillery of any kind. Just to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd also inquire if we could have some assistance again on dates, as to what time-period we're now talking about, when these supposedly 122-millimetre howitzers were put in position, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dates are important, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Petkovic, what we are marking here on several documents, what time-period exactly are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be precise, this is a time-period from the end of 1992, when the ABiH first obtained howitzers in the operation of liberating Mostar, and then they got two or three howitzers from the area of Mostar. I don't know how many 105-millimetre howitzers exactly they had, three or five, but they were in the area of Gnojnica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from 1992 on. But when I was mentioning the HVO, I had in mind the HVO south of Capljina all the way to Dreznica. So the area of the HVO is much larger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Petkovic, if we disregard Capljina, which isn't on this map, tell us, during the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, what was the balance of forces -- of artillery forces in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ratio between the Serbian artillery and the HVO would have been the same, and whereas the ratio between the HVO and the ABiH, especially from the 30th of June on, was 2:1 in favour of the HVO. Apart from the 41st Brigade, we can see that the Prosecution marked, that there was also the 47th Brigade and the 48th Brigade, so the ABiH had three brigades where they formerly only had one. So they must have come from somewhere. They were established in this area, and they were included in the structure of the ABiH in these areas. So we mustn't forget that there were three ABiH brigades there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you said, in fact, that the Serbs had eight times more artillery as the HVO, whereas the HVO had two and a half times more artillery than the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please mark Rosci here on this map and what can be found there. Who controlled Rosci?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] This is the area of Rosci, the Rosci Mountains. How do you want me to mark --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mark a number 1 where the artillery is. And whose artillery.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the artillery of the VRS. It's in the area of the Rosci Mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Show us on this map, General, which roads leave the western part of Mostar and go westward? There are two roads.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 [marks] is the road from Mostar. I forget what the name of this suburb is. It isn't the main road; it's just an auxiliary road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It goes via Goranci?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I forgot. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the other?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And road number 2 [marks] is the main road Mostar-Siroki Brijeg and on. Another road diverges from it and goes left to Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could the VRS artillery target these two roads leading out of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could the ABiH artillery target these two roads?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were also able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please mark on this map the positions of the VRS. You don't have to be very precise. Just mark roughly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. The remainder of the area to Mount Rosci and towards Blagaj cannot be seen on this map. It's below Velez Mount.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Please sign, and I also would like an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Do you want me to mark these positions in some manner?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Put "VRS."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The marked version of page 2 of document 3D03798 shall be given Exhibit IC01192. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the previous map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, from the positions of the VRS, that is, their artillery, but also from the positions of the artillery of the ABiH artillery, was Western Mostar just as encircled as that portion of the forces of the ABiH that was between the HVO and the VRS with a free passage to the north? Were they able to target with their artillery every road leading westward from the city?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Howitzers, 122-millimetre, have a range of 12 kilometres, a tank cannon 6 to 7 kilometres, mortars also about 6 kilometres, so they were able to target everything within range if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the HVO ever issue orders to shoot at civilians going -- moving along the axis north-south to Blagaj, et cetera, or is there any information from international forces that civilians were shot at?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that there were two observation points north of Mostar, but civilians were never targeted. Unfortunately, the communication of the ABiH leading northward wasn't targeted often, but it's very difficult to shoot at moving vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look at document 3D00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misunderstood, General. On line 3, page 45, you say that there were two observation points. Who was there, who was holding them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that there were observers on the HVO side that observed the entire area. Also, on the VRS side there were observers, and on the ABiH side, because you must have observers for the artillery. Otherwise, artillery is of no use to you. For artillery to be able to open fire, they must have observers or scouts who observe the enemy. Every side had such artillery observers monitoring the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to the transcript. I'll just read out to you what was recorded. General Petkovic, please say whether you really said that.
