On page 45, starting from line 2, the English text reads that General Petkovic said: [In English] "Unfortunately, the communication of the ABiH leading northward wasn't targeted often, but it's very difficult to shoot at moving vehicles." [Interpretation] Tell us, General, are these really your words? Did you say "unfortunate"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the HVO never even fired at certain troop movements of the ABiH from Bijelo Polje northward, let alone that they would dare open fire at civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at document 3D00740, please. It's an exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. The moment we get the next document on the screen, we're going to lose this current map that we have with the marking. Would you like a number for it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please give us a number for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked version of document P11081 shall be given Exhibit IC01193. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I don't know if Mr. Praljak is going to continue with the maps and the artillery positions, but you will recall that last week I asked you questions about these maps, and I had also asked questions to other witnesses, because my concern is the following, and what I want to do here is explain how relevant my question is. We have documents. The documents are of an international source. There were bombing from the HVO, and there were victims, according to these documents. Now, as a criminal judge, it is necessary for me to know the date of the bombing, who was in the artillery, who was holding the Howitzer or the mortar, so that we can draw a conclusion without -- beyond a reasonable doubt that there were victims, and the victims were the victims of fire from HVO. And I have to be 100 per cent sure, because I cannot speculate and I cannot just risk suppositions here. Why do I say this? Because my experience of international justice has demonstrated that appearances can fool you. Remember Nuremberg. In the indictment, the Germans accused were charged with cutting, and the prosecutor, the Soviet prosecutor, and the judge, the Soviet judge, did not want this to be discussed. At the request of the German Defence team, three witnesses testified that it wasn't the Germans who had killed the Polish officers, but the Soviet troops. So when something looks like something, I always check, because at the time of decision we cannot afford to make a mistake, because there will be an impact, and that's why I asked you questions, and that's why I asked where the artillery was positioned. I wanted to know what the range of the cannons was, and I wanted to know whether fire, either from ABiH or from VRS, could possibly reach Eastern Mostar. Now, I'm asking the question again. As far as you know, General Petkovic, given the positions that you have described - that we've seen on the maps - was it possible for fire to reach Eastern Mostar? I'm talking about fire either from ABiH or VRS or HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, let me start by saying that civilians would have come to harm if there hadn't been any shelling. In artillery, it is usual to say, Shoot at the target observed, and the target is an enemy soldier, a group of soldiers, materiel, a command post, and et cetera. And now to your question. I marked the positions of the VRS artillery. Each position -- from each position of theirs, it was possible to target Eastern Mostar. All positions of the ABiH were in range of the HVO positions in Mostar, and vice versa. So the HVO positions were such that they could open fire on all these targets. In other words, all three sides had their respective positions along the front-line from the Bijela Bridge to Blagaj, and it was possible, from all these positions, to open fire at enemy targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to intervene with regard to the first sentence of the general's reply. It starts on page 47. I'm not able to locate it in the other transcript because the line references are different. So the first sentence of the general's answer was if there hadn't been -- correction. There was no shelling, in order to avoid civilians coming to harm. We have now found the line reference. It's page 47, lines 21 to 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly. I wanted to assist you on that, and maybe it's -- I have noticed the same thing. I think there's something wrong there. Perhaps you want to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript reads literally: [In English] "Let me start by saying that civilians would have come to harm if there hadn't been any shelling." [Interpretation] Whereas the general actually said that there wasn't any shelling, to avoid hitting civilians, meaning that there was no shelling to avoid civilian casualties. But the general can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the general please rephrase? We cannot understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the interpreters are asking you to repeat your reply. Start from the beginning and speak slowly, and do monitor the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the artillery didn't shell in order to hit civilians or to harm the civilian population in any way. The artillery of all three sides in the area opened fire, first and foremost, in fact, only against known military targets, and there are various types of military targets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, all the artillery positions that we saw of the VRS, was it possible to fire on both sides of Mostar, the western and the eastern side, from those positions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible to do so, and even further to the west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: As for the ABiH artillery, could they open fire on the western side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I forgot to say or ask whether the Bijela Bridge was under the control of the ABiH in April - that's the first date - and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Bijela Bridge was under the control of the ABiH, under the control of the 4th Battalion of the 41st Mostar Brigade. This was continually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If the level of the lake fell, was the road around the Bijelo Valley passable?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the road that used to be used, and when the level of the water would fall, that route was, in fact, practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the 30th of June, who had control of the dams on the Neretva River to the north of Mostar? Who could regulate the level of the water?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 30th of June, Your Honours, 1993, all the dams on the Neretva River were under the control of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I was hoping we would get there, but so far we've only heard that it was possible to lower the water sufficiently that the old bridge would be exposed. But unless I'm mistaken, and if I'm wrong, I'm sure I'll be corrected, there's been no evidence, and I'm wondering whether Mr. Praljak will ask whether, in fact, that was ever done, or is this all just a matter of speculation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, try and be more specific so that there is no ambiguity or any grey areas. I would like to let you to know that you have five minutes left, General Praljak, so make sure that you finish in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a lot of time is wasted on procedure, unfortunately, putting maps on the ELMO, and so on and so forth. But I'll answer this: Why should I prove whether the ABiH was in a position to lower the level of the water? And we saw that it raised the level of the water and, in fact, flood the entire area. Why should I have to prove that they might not lower the water-level and open up the road? If you could have lunch, but you don't, is that your problem? What are we dealing with here? What is it that the Prosecution wants? I don't understand. If they had control over the dams, and the witness said that was the case, then the issue as to whether they want to go over the bridge or if they wanted to go by a roundabout way, well, that's a matter of what they want to do. Will they go over the hills? So my question is: Is it possible that they went in that way? Is it possible that they could use artillery to have control over the western exits? The Prosecution also claims, for example, the HVO could have control over the road that went in the direction of the north. Please, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, would you like to answer this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the ABiH, as of the September 1992 [as interpreted], would constantly let water out of the Salakovac Dam. They flooded the entire area up until the dam of the Mostar hydroelectric plant, and thus they placed under threat part of an area under the HVO near the nun's home, but they also posed a threat to the Mostar Dam. And the consequences for the town of Mostar could have been extremely serious.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, "September 1992" is what I see here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] September 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that please be corrected, then. 3D00740. Could we see that document? 3D00740.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this document? Are you familiar with what the contents of the document are? What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm familiar with this document. It's already been shown in the courtroom on a number of occasions, and the HVO felt the consequences of this document in the field. This is a combat order from the 4th Corps Command according to which the western part of Mostar and other parts of -- the remaining parts of Mostar should be placed under the control of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at item 4, and please explain the following for me: What is the artillery group from the Rosci area? Whose artillery is concerned? What is being directed at the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group mentioned by Arif Pasalic is a group from the VRS on the Rosci Mountain, and it has been marked under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that in September and in October, the offensive action of the ABiH against the town of Mostar was supported by the RS artillery from the positions around Mostar and mainly from the position of Rosci Mountain, because that is the best place from which to control the western part of Mostar and the hill of Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 4D00625. It's a map that's already an exhibit. I just have one question about this. 4D00625.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who drew this map, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My second question: When you've marked these areas in blue, green and red, does this mean - and Judge Trechsel asked you about this - does this mean that those areas are under the control of the army or is the army only present at the demarcation lines?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army is present at the demarcation lines, and the area was taken to be the area that the first, second, or third government had under its control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So the road from the north to the south and to the eastern part of Mostar from Blagaj, via Bijelo Polje, the Bijelo Most and Jablanica and Konjic, was this road always open to traffic, to members of the ABiH who came from the north as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People used these routes -- this route, and ABiH brigades also used these routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, when you plan for an attack, what must the balance of the forces be, the ratio between those attacking and those defending?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the JNA rule was that you shouldn't launch an attack unless the balance of forces were 3:1 in favour of those launching the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What was the balance of forces in Central Bosnia, Konjic, Jablanica, and Mostar? What was the ratio of forces between the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, from April 1993 until the end of the year, the ratio was between 5:1 in favour of the armija and even sometimes 8:1 for the armija, ABiH. It depended on which areas they had taken from the HVO. HVO forces would be expelled from that area, so their forces were reduced and the ABiH forces were increased.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You've explained what these colours mean for the map. Could we have an IC number for this map, and this is in relation to the questions that I have put.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, General Petkovic, could you mark the map with the numbers 1, 2, 3, these areas that are depicting various colours? What did you say about these three colours. Does the army control and who?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armija, the army, is at the first lines, and the government controls the depth. Under 1, the red colour, depicts the area under the VRS. The green area represents the area that was under the Bosniak Muslim authorities. And the blue area was under the HVO authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you sign the map, please, and could you please mark the map with those numbers? Could we also have an IC number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please. General Petkovic, you haven't marked 1, 2 and 3. Please mark these.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And sign it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I used the wrong pen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked portion of document 4D00625 shall be given Exhibit IC01194. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Petkovic, now I have a question before I ask Their Honours for some time. As deputy commander, when I was in command, did you issue orders? That's my first question. And, two: Did you expect those orders to be executed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I issued orders, and the orders -- well, one would have expected them to be carried out, because if you fail to carry out an order, everyone will be held accountable by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So did this rule apply to General Zarko Tole?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Tole also had to be held to account by you for carrying out orders that he had signed. That's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, have you no time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may make a request. We were afraid that there wouldn't be sufficient time, because in your decision you only granted us an hour and 20 minutes for cross-examination. General Praljak selected a certain number of topics, and I hope he'll be able to conclude with these topics in 20 to 25 minutes' time. If it's not possible to proceed in any other way, we'll deduct this from the time that we were keeping for future use. So I'm asking you whether General Praljak could be granted additional time for his cross-examination, because the procedure has been a little more lengthy than expected today, through no fault of our own. If you believe that he can't be granted additional time for his cross-examination, please allow him to use the amount of time he needs, 20 to 25 minutes, by deducting that time from the time we still have at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues, and maybe I shall tell you what my personal view is. I shall turn to my colleagues right now and ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Judges deliberate on the matter: General Praljak, are your questions new questions? Because the Trial Chamber sees that as regards the questions that you have put, these have been addressed already. You have to provide added value. Are there any new questions which have a high added value which you would like to put? Because if you just want to go over the same ground, then we're wasting our ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, there are certain clarifications that have to do with certain issues that haven't been clarified, certain issues that aren't quite clear. There's the Jeremy Bowen extract or film, video, that I want to put questions about. So I think that new questions that would add value to what has already been said might be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My dear colleague, Ms. Nika Pinter, was very carefully, very carefully analysing each topic which Mr. Praljak is planning to raise, and I can assure you that according to our analysis, really each topic he would raise was in a way and rather directly, more directly or less directly, raised during either direct or Your Honour's question. And it is exactly what General Praljak said, where we felt that there are certain facts connected to the raised issues, and those issues need to be elaborated more in details, those questions -- better to say such questions are on Mr. Praljak's list, and, of course, all restricted by the military questions. And I really want to say that what I just said is on good-faith basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I seem to have missed something, then, because the map we have seen last has been before us now at least for the third time, and this had been put to this witness -- before this witness by the President, in his interrogation. And I must missed what new was added now when the same map was put before the witness by Mr. Praljak. Perhaps you can clarify this, because I would not want to disagree on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I think that it's quite clear -- if you compare the transcript of previous discussions of this map, I think it's quite clear that now General Praljak has gone into more details, because it is only now, on the basis of General Petkovic's answer, that it is quite clear as to where the other side was present, the VRS and the Muslim side. It's quite clear where they had their artillery positions. So this additional step has been made, the situation has been geographically specified, and we have realised that from all those positions it was not a problem to fire on Mostar, which was within range of those artillery positions. If you're asking me about the last map that we have just had a look at, well, there was an additional explanation concerning the fact that these three areas, depicted in different colours, are areas in which the army didn't have control over the entire territory. That's not what the colours mean. In fact, we had to confirm this, because it wasn't clear. It's not quite clear on the basis of the image, if you're not familiar with the background. And there were quite specific questions put by the Judges about this matter, so we thought that it was necessary to clarify this once and for all. So we have clarified who was positioned at those locations. That was the additional question -- the new question. I don't see any repetition, apart from the fact that it was sometimes necessary to repeat certain things to determine what has been demonstrated so far and what remains or remained to be demonstrated. That can be somewhat confusing, because you have to go over the same ground sometimes for this purpose. There is another dilemma. I've spoken to General Praljak about this on a number of occasions. You remember that the Prosecution, and I'm not criticising for this, but the Prosecution regularly objects when foundations haven't been laid for certain questions. We have discussed this on a number of occasions, and in my opinion General Praljak always lays the foundations, and the foundation in this case has to do with prior discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues and ask whether they agree to grant an extra 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Trial Chamber unanimously grants you 20 extra minutes, but this goes against your time credit. I feel that all the questions you have put are not questions which should be put during cross-examination. These questions should be put during examination-in-chief, and I agree with the Prosecutor in this regard. And the Prosecutor explained this in his formal written submissions. All this should be addressed during the examination-in-chief. This is not in line with the spirits of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Since you have two hours and 28 minutes left, this will be taken off that allotted time. That is why I agree with my colleagues on this point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may briefly reply to Mr. Kovacic. If you say that it is sometimes necessary to repeat -- to recapitulate, I would not agree. I don't think that here this is necessary, and I would hope that Mr. Praljak, in going on with the questioning, will not follow the maxim that it is sometimes useful to repeat, simply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, General Praljak. You have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. P06365. That's a television clip by Jeremy Bowen, a journalist, so I'd like to show the extract where he says that civilians are being expelled from Western Mostar to Eastern Mostar at night, yes. General Petkovic, take a close look, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "The Reporter: ... Croats. They had to cross the River Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of rope and planks. Bosnian soldiers told them which way to go --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw everybody's attention to the shadows.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "The Reporter: The Croats were shooting at the people they just made refugees. Only a few hours before, until the Croat gangs had come for them and forced them over the front-line --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is as far as I want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, while this was being shot, was there any electricity in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no light source to be seen anywhere, which means wherever they were shooting, there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that day can be turned into night, which is known as American night, in movie-making by usually special filters, infrared filters? So an IC filter turns day into night, and shadows originating from unknown lamps, in a city without electricity, are like this? Have you heard of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of such false nights. It is illogical, though, that you can see people moving about allegedly at night and still casting a shadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We spoke at that time about this topic. What was the purpose of making such a video-clip of forging reality, if I may call it? What was Mr. Bowen's aim?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. How can this witness possibly testify about what Mr. Bowen's state of mind was? Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is how Mr. Bowen could give us such video. The Prosecutor should have called somebody else to verify the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The burden is on the Prosecution. The Prosecution used the video, which we only lately understood that this cannot be right, because the shadow cannot be seen in the dark. Simple as that. And now the Prosecutor is objecting. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right, I am objecting. Mr. Kovacic, don't try to shift the issue. The issue -- my objection was: This witness cannot possibly speculate as to what Mr. Bowen's intention or state of mind was, cannot possibly do that, and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, yes, it is better if you rephrase your question. You should have put a very neutral question, whereas the way you put the question was a way of calling for the answer. When I agree with Mr. Scott, I say so. When I disagree with him, I say so also. In this instance, I agree with him. You cannot draw conclusions about Mr. Bowen's intentions, so put the question to the witness in another way. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, Your Honours. It's a mistake I made because of a shortage of time. I analysed this video with expert professionals, and I could spend as much as an hour on it, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, Mr. Petkovic, we saw people crossing mountains, we saw shadows in a city without electricity, so what can you say about the time when this video was made, and what can you say about the conversations we had back then about Mr. Bowen's role?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm still objecting the question. I don't care if they speculated in 2010 or they speculated in 1993. In either case, they can't speculate as to what Mr. Bowen's intention was. It doesn't matter but -- that we've shifted the time and gone back in time. It's still speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It very much depends on what is Mr. Petkovic about to say. He already said three words on the beginning of the sentence, so I have the feeling that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was an awkward question. It was extremely awkward, the one that was put by General Praljak. General Petkovic, we've just seen a video where we could see shadows. That's the only question. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was made in the city of Mostar in August 1993, when, after the talk that Mr. Bowen had with Mr. Delic, which he mentioned himself, Mr. Bowen set off for Mostar, and this was before the start of the military operation. So Mr. Bowen was probably -- it was his intention to be a first to report about the ABiH having taken Mostar, but it didn't happen. So he probably -- he went back to England to take a vacation, and then he came back in September/October to mark the historic achievement of the ABiH, the taking of Western Mostar, but that failed too. And then he produced something else, something that would look nice and that he could send out to the world, but he didn't show the most important thing. And that's why he --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Mr. Petkovic just confirmed the exact basis for my objections all along. He's done nothing but speculation, pure speculation, that Mr. Bowen didn't get what he wanted, he went back to London, he had a vacation, he came back a second time, he probably didn't get what he wanted. This is nonsense. I move to strike it. My original objection should have been sustained and he should not have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please. Since that has to do with the interpretation, I think I should be the first to say something and help assist everybody. Mr. Scott rose a bit too soon, and he didn't give the interpreters a chance to interpret Mr. Petkovic's last sentence. And what Mr. Petkovic said was that Mr. Jeremy Bowen stated the following himself -- now I've been misinterpreted. I didn't say that he stated the following, but what I said was that Mr. Petkovic's words about Mr. Bowen were the words that Mr. Bowen said himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already seen this video. It's not the first time that we see it. I must tell you that I hadn't noticed the shadows, and I must tell you that before this question was put to you around 10 minutes past 5.00 p.m., this was on my mind and I thought that this had been shot at night. I, therefore, thought that the journalist was showing what was happening at night in Mostar, people who were leaving, people who were putting their lives on the line. At no point in time had I imagined that this could have been shot in the afternoon. But if that is the case, if this has been shot in the afternoon, this is a way of forging the truth, and that is a serious matter. I assume this video was broadcast in the media and the people watching this thought that this happened at night. A while ago you said something which I hear for the first time. This is something I knew nothing about. You said that Mr. Bowen met Mr. Delic. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I attentively listened to Mr. Bowen's testimony here. He contacted Delic and then left Sarajevo, and then a man by the name of Kovacevic, I believe, a member of the ABiH, received him when he left Sarajevo. He took him to Jablanica, and then Mr. Bowen was sent to what was known as the mule trail to produce footage about that, although he could have arrived at Mostar differently. At that time, Mr. Delic planned the Neretva 93 operation, and obviously he expected to take Western Mostar in August, or until mid-September, at worse, but that failed. And then Mr. Bowen himself said that he returned to England and then returned to the area of Mostar in late September or early October, when there really was fierce fighting in Mostar. And according to me, he was in a position to make footage of the fighting at Hum, where the ABiH had 30 to 40 casualties in the operation of taking Hum, but he was unable to produce anything else except for the footage involving Pasalic, clean-shaven, having a conversation with him. And my conclusion from his testimony is that it had been his initial intention to be the first to publish the news that the ABiH has taken Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that I cannot continue analysing this footage with Mr. Petkovic, because if I were in the position to testify about this being a movie director -- former movie director and engineer of electrical engineering, but, anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. Well, Mr. Praljak, you're not in a position to testify. You've already done that, and you can't testify now. Again, everything Mr. Petkovic has said in the last five minutes is pure speculation, whether it's what Mr. Delic thought at a given time or what conversations may or may not -- this kind of speculation should not be allowed. Any witness could come here and speculate all afternoon long, and it doesn't -- it's a poor usage of time, as Judge Trechsel has pointed out. This is sheer speculation. This is Mr. Petkovic just going on in a fantasy world.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I think that General Petkovic, who was present in this courtroom regularly and listened to all witness statements, has the right to draw his conclusions as to the testimonies of individual witnesses. I would like to remind of the fact that the testimony of Mr. Thornberry, who spoke here about how the media campaign was organised to raise the sensitivity of Western European -- the Western European public, with regard to this conflict, and pressurised the governments to change their attitude towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Mr. Thornberry's testimony fits perfectly in the picture of Mr. Jeremy Bowen's activities in the area, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, a while ago I seem to have heard you say that Mr. Bowen had declared he had seen Mr. Delic. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that at the beginning of his testimony, he spoke about the departure from Sarajevo and that he came to meet General Delic. What they did, I don't know, but that's what Mr. Bowen stated here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, let me quote to you what he actually says, and this is on page 12778, line 21 and following. I quote: "Before Mostar, I went to the office of Rasim Delic in Sarajevo, for example, and we got no information about those kind of things." This is practically the only reference of any contact between Mr. Bowen and -- well, actually, it does not say that there is a contact with Mr. Delic. So probably I have not searched well enough, but to this moment I cannot find confirmation for what you have told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 23rd of January, 2007, page 12778 of the transcript of Jeremy Bowen's testimony, the following is stated: "Before I went to Mostar, I went to Rasim Delic's office in Sarajevo." So, therefore -- the line is line 22. And on that occasion, I can't now go through the entire transcript, but a direct reference is made to Rasim Delic and to the contact Jeremy Bowen had with him, and this is what General Petkovic said. He said that that's what Bowen said, so in this very courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Counsel. That's exactly the lines that I have read a few minutes ago. I don't know why you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may add one sentence. My colleague checked what you said in the transcript, and as we have understood this part of the cited statement of Mr. Bowen is he met Delic. In our colloquial language, when I said that I visited your office, Your Honour, for example, your chambers, that means that I met you. This is how every average person understands that. I agree with you that in forensic analysis, yes, maybe that wouldn't be sufficient. Maybe we would need one extra step, And there I have seen this person. But when we said in colloquial language, I visited Mr. Khan's office, that means I met him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, it's just that Mr. Bowen doesn't speak your common-law -- everyday language, but he comes from England, and, I mean, this, it doesn't really -- I am not convinced at all of your explanation. That's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, not to move on. I think the most important question is not about this Delic issue but if the general can give an opinion as to this particular video. Having seen it, does he have an opinion whether it's accurate, whether it accurately reflects the situation as it was at the particular time, given the logistics, given the electricity, and so on and so forth. That is the critical question that needs to be answered. I'm not sure it was answered or was ever asked. And then I think we should just move on. But I think that is the critical aspect of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree. The issue is whether the witness can testify about the intentions of Mr. Bowen. That was put, raised an objection, and I'm glad to hear that you are not of a different opinion, and that the way you have put the question is absolutely -- I'm in full agreement with that. Perhaps, Mr. Petkovic, you are able to say something about the weather in August of 1993, and, in particular, about moonlight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, in August in Mostar, every year, in 1993, too, the weather is very hot, it's very sunny, it's almost 35 degrees or even more in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When does night fall? At what time does night fall?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your opinion, does this mean that the night we can see here isn't really night, it's not nighttime, it's daytime, but transformed into night-time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He can't say that, Your Honour. He can't say that. It's just speculation again. Looking at this, all I can do is -- all Mr. Petkovic can do is the same thing all of us in the courtroom can do. He can look at that and say, Well, it looks like it has a greenish tint to it and there's some shadows. It shows what it shows, but he can't add anything to that. It's sheer -- was he there when this video was taken? Was he standing on the spot where Mr. Bowen was and when the people were coming across the bridge from West Mostar? Was he standing there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But such shadows are not possible, regardless of the extent to which we say that night-time -- at night-time it was visible or not visible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on. P01139, please. It has to do with the ultimatum. I have two short questions about this. P01139. Could we have it on the screen, please. P01139, it's the famous ultimatum that was referred to in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, General, please just have a look at -- further down towards the bottom. There are two items. Have a look at item 5. What does item 5 say? Have a look at what it says.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the commands of the armed forces of the HVO at the level of OZ brigades. It says that those commands have to be joined by ABiH officers, and the ratio has to be a ratio that takes into consideration the number of soldiers at the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If in Central Bosnia there are more ABiH soldiers in the battle-field than HVO soldiers, who will form the majority in the joint command?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, members of the Muslim people or, rather, members of the ABiH, and the percentage of Bosniaks or the ABiH members would have to be greater by the same percentage that there were more ABiH soldiers than HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this a fair approach or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 5 says that this is the implementation of an agreement on joint commands. If we're reaching an agreement on joint commands, then we won't threaten each other, if we manage to reach such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, item 7, what does this so-called ultimatum start with? How does it start?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that commanders of operative zones have the obligation to initiate talks with the commanders of the ABiH in order to find the best ways of setting up joint commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the course of your life, have you ever heard about an ultimatum that starts with a reference to discussions, to the initiation of talks?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an invitation to hold discussions in order to find a common solution, a joint solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: A very brief question now. Judge Antonetti was very curious about how I had taken over your role and you became the second in command, so my question is: On the 19th of April, 1992, when you became the chief of the HVO Main Staff, was I your subordinate, as the commander of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander at that time, yes, you were subordinated to me at that forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did that present a problem when it came to communication, when it came to who issued orders to whom, or under the circumstances was this not of such importance to us, it was of less importance to us than it would have been in a normal army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't create any problems, we didn't create any problems -- at least I didn't create any problems when you arrived down there and when you became engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know anything about this? Were you informed? Was I with you at the front-line? Did I act without your knowledge? Did I act against you? Was there a problem of any kind that occurred between us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you never acted against me, because you were there performing your duties for the territory where you had been born, for a territory in which you had been born, a territory where you had lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have an entire new subject, but I have two or three more questions. What's the combat part of the HVO army, and what's the non-combat part?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military part, the combat part of the HVO is in the direct chain of command and from the Supreme Commander of the Main Staff of operative zones, down to brigades, to battalions, to companies, to platoons, to squads; so that's the entire structure that is involved at the combat lines, at the front-lines, so that is the military structure and it is at such locations that they perform their duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm not sure the transcript is correct, because the general said: [In English] "The non-military part of the HVO is in the Supreme Command and from the Supreme Command to the operating zones," et cetera. [Interpretation] As far as I understood, the general he said that that was the military part of the HVO, and when talking about the chain of command he mentioned the Main Staff. So perhaps the general could repeat that so that it doesn't seem as if he didn't to want to speak about the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the military part is represented by units of the HVO, it includes units of the HVO that organised into brigades, battalions, military districts, which are under the command of the supreme commander, the Main Staff, the operative zone brigade commanders, brigade commanders, battalion commanders, company commanders, and squad commanders. So that is the military part that goes to the front-lines and is engaged in combat tasks at those lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what is the non-military part?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-military part would be all the so-called service sectors that other departments are involved in, other bodies are involved in, for the needs of the combat part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you list them, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-military part would include medical care, logistics support, security for units, intelligence, providing intelligence, and so on and so forth. So they assist the combat component.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who is in command of the combat component, and who is in command of the non-military HVO component ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that I have already said that the combat component is under the command of command structures, starting with the supreme commander, then you have the Main Staff, the operative zone, the brigade, and then you have lower-level units. The non-combat component -- the non-combat component includes the Ministry of Defence, other structures, right down to operative zones and brigades. So those are the non-combat components of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I fear there is a little bit of confusion here. What you have now answered, distinguishing combat and non-combat, that makes sense, but earlier on the question was military and non-military, and what you have referred to now, all these services, logistics, intelligence, security, they are military, but non-combat; isn't that what you were telling us? I see our interpretation police chief. Ms. Tomanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the problem has to do with the interpretation. At one point in time, the term "non-combat" is used, and the other -- on other occasions "non-military" is used. I think "non-combat" should be used at all times, because the general didn't make any distinction between military and non-military structures, but between combat and non-combat instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters comment: The interpreter can confirm what Counsel has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a combat and non-combat component to a military structure. That is what one has to bear in mind. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is a valuable clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it would be good to take a break. It is, anyway, time for a break. And then maybe the general could reorganise and wisely use those six minutes -- seven minutes. Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume. Before I give the floor back to you, I'm sure you all know that we will be sitting tomorrow morning at 9.00, that is, Tuesday, and Thursday afternoon. I would like to make it clear that we will stop at 6.00, 6.00 p.m., on Thursday. I don't know why we are sitting tomorrow morning, because we had been scheduled to sit in the afternoon. Judge Mindua is sitting in the Tolimir case, and I am sitting on the Seselj case, together with two other Judges who are sitting on the Karadzic and Stanisic cases, so we need to juggle with the hearings because the Judges have several cases simultaneously, which is very tiring. In light of the completion strategy, we need, however, organise things in this manner. I will let you know by the minute if there are any changes in the courtrooms or any other information. We all do what we can to make sure that this works out well. You have seven minutes left, Mr. Praljak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Let us go through this quickly, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: The Security Service, health-care inside the HVO, logistics, information propaganda, military police, are these combat or non-combat components, and who manages them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are non-combat components, unsecured -- they are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, the last part of his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please repeat once more. Are these services [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are single services, individual services, or separate services. The health-care is run by the head of the Health-Care Department, and the structure SIS is run by the assistant head of security. Logistics is in the responsibility of the assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may intervene with regard to the first sentence of General Petkovic's reply, which isn't correctly interpreted. The question was whether they are single services. The translations given are not adequate. It should be "unique."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We don't agree with that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the interpreters wanted you to change the position of your microphones, because they have a problem with it. Thank you, Usher. General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Petkovic, behind you there is a map. It is IC00219. It's an exhibit. And here's my question: Are you familiar with that map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In April, in accordance with the documents produced here or shown here, did the units of the ABiH plan to attack the western part of Mostar, as shown by the green arrows on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was based on their orders dated the 19th and the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The attack of the ABiH on the 9th of May, was it carried out for a major part along these axes shown here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the only possible axes, bearing in mind the situation that prevailed then in the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: A series of buildings and facilities are listed here which the ABiH has taken possession of for their needs. Did they ever talk to you about that or did they do that without having reached an agreement with you, including Vranica, where they put up their Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- disposing of facilities and buildings are not within the remit of the Main Staff. The correct procedure was to take possession of a building you must file a request for the requisition of such a building or facility, but the ABiH never filed such an application. They simply took possession of vacated facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please sign this map, and let us submit it to the Trial Chamber then.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I be given a pen, other than the one that I have already?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: While we're waiting, please find 3D3799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, as my colleague has just told me, you haven't annotated the map in any way. The map has been admitted. Why do you wish to sign it? Why did General Praljak ask for a number? Because this map has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see 3D3799, please. 3D3799, that's a document dated the 1st of April, 1994 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We see, as signatories, the collegium of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina. General, did you have an opportunity to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this before. I didn't have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know what all three sides signed about the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cutileiro Plan offered the following structure: All three sides, that is, the Croatian, Serb, and Bosnian, should have the same status, and Bosnia should be territorially organised into entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document and tell me whether it follows from it that the collegium of the MUP with the Serbs and the Bosniaks took the decision to split the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a Serb and a Muslim component and whether that was based on an agreement with Mr. Izetbegovic, because we can see Mr. Delimustafic's signature here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document reads that the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised into three -- or as three wholes, three components, on the basis of the Cutileiro Plan, and each of these would be some kind of organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what would -- and what else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably all other institutions -- common institutions should be organised along the same lines as the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are very, very strongly overlapping, so the interpreters cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the more so, General Praljak, since you have no time left, put your last question. Your time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My last question. Just a small correction, General, to somebody's question. I don't recall whose. You said, General, that the war in Central Bosnia was such that everything became much worse after Totic and his escort had been arrested. What was this about? We saw some photographs of that arrest.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totic was intercepted and arrested, and four of his escorts, four persons escorting him, were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When was that, and who was Totic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of April, 1994. He was the commander of the Zenica Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the ABiH, and some people say that they were Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my last question. Thank you, General, for your answers. Your Honours, thank you for your time and patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may intervene right now. On page 77, line 20, the transcript reads that the document is 3D3799, that this document is dated 1st of April, 1994. This is very confusing, because the actual date is the 1st of April, 1992. I don't know whether the general misspoke or something, but, anyway, it is clear the document reads "1992."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the document reads the "1st of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness confirms. After this remark, I would also ask the Trial Chamber's permission for General Praljak to address the Chamber with a request of his, which he has put in writing, but he would like to inform you of some decisions he made and the reasons for these decisions. And then we will formulate his position in writing so as not to use more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 6, page 79, it's not the 15th of April, 1994, but 15th of April, 1993. Is that right, General Petkovic? Mr. Totic was abducted on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of "arrested," I said, "abducted." I shall turn to my colleagues to see whether they agree that Mr. Praljak takes the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Trial Chamber holds that it is for the counsel to intervene, not for the accused. Are there any reasons for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whether there are reasons or not is for you to decide. It is the Defence's position that the accused, in line with the basic human rights, has the right to speak, and that includes the courtroom, too. He will not venture into legal analyses, but I don't doubt that he has the right that -- the right to address the Trial Chamber personally, not through his Defence counsel, because it's about a problem that bears heavily upon him, and he took some decisions with regard to this trial. And, therefore, it is our position that he should address the Trial Chamber in person, state his decisions, and give the reasons why he decided to do so at this very moment. So to speak no longer, I think that it is his right to address the Trial Chamber in person. Of course, it's for the Trial Chamber to say, Not now, but, I don't know, tomorrow, first time in the morning, or whenever, but this seems to be a convenient moment because my colleague can hardly do anything valuable in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you wish to talk about, the Olympic Games, the conditions in detention, the light bulbs that are missing in his cell, whatever difficulties he wishes to share with us, or does it have to do with the procedure? The Judges would just like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the general should speak about that himself. But as you're asking me, I will say that General Praljak, after due consideration, and after assessing many circumstances and consulting his lawyers and other persons, decided to put an end to his active participation in these proceedings and refrain from coming to the courtroom in the days to come because he wishes to show that he's unwilling to participate in something which he cannot accept due to the method -- for methodological reasons. And I'll come back to what I've already said. I believe that in these matters, it is an inalienable right of the accused which is respected in other courts to address the Trial Chamber directly. I can say that in the national jurisdiction of my country and as far as I've been able to conclude in my analysis, in other national jurisdictions, that is also possible, of course, if we respect the rules and if you stay decent, et cetera. But here, in this Tribunal, too, the accused have had the opportunity to explain their views to the Trial Chambers in their cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak would like to explain to us why he will not be attending the court hearing of the next few days. I believe that that is what he would like to talk to us about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure that it's a matter of the next few days. For the moment, the general has decided to no longer participate in the trial, to withdraw, to remain in the Detention Unit while proceedings are ongoing. He knows that he has the opportunity of appearing here, but he will not do so. As to whether that will last for a few days or until the end of the trial, well, it all depends on how things unfold, and naturally it also depends on his subjective understanding of the matter. Everyone takes decisions on the basis of the facts, as interpreted by the person in question. And I believe that it is the accused's right to state that that is his position, and the Trial Chamber should act in a bona fide manner and listen to what the accused has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall turn to my colleagues and ask them what they think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen the Trial Chamber deliberate on the matter. In the majority, the Trial Chamber has decided that General Praljak can explain to us why it is he no [as interpreted] wishes to come to the courtroom. But the Trial Chamber shall not take a position on Mr. Praljak's stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is my duty to state openly that I am the one dissenting in the Chamber, and I do this because I do not see any basis for a right of an accused to address the Chamber beyond what has been put before the Appeals Chamber, and the Appeals Chamber has given two rulings, actually, on this. It is perhaps a bit formalistic, I will admit that, but I think that's how the procedure ought to be regulated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have put all this in writing. I have drafted about 11 pages on the matter, and I will be a lot briefer here. I apologise to the interpreters. Sometimes the text is somewhat confused, but the Judges will be provided with a full translation of the text. It's a matter of acts of procedure and such matters of extreme importance when a certain social structure is breaking up: How does one act? At the time of the French Revolution, when the Nazi era appears, in times of fascism, in times of communism, how should one act in war, in wartime? How should one avoid committing errors, having wrong thoughts, being guilty of omissions? I have disturbed the Chamber with an issue concerning Heisenberg, who asked Planck about the rise of Nazism in Germany. And I think I have read all the relevant literature about this matter, and in the literature on the matter, it says that each and every individual has to decide -- or, rather, decides about how to act when three variables are put in the balance: courage and the unacceptability of being passive within a system, a given system, and in the light of expected punishment -- anticipated punishment. Why are such things said? Because, in my opinion, the cumulative development of minor and negative procedures in this trial has led me to a position which I can no longer accept this. The Prosecution's practice has been demonstrated in books. In the book of Carla Del Ponte, for example, one has a demonstration of the practice followed by the Prosecution, Carla Del Ponte, the Prosecutor. We can find similar things in the book written by Florence Hartmann, "Peace and Punishment." In many cases, the indictment is drafted in order to satisfy certain political objectives, the interests of various parties that aren't clear, it satisfies things that go on behind the scene, and all this results in putting into question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You said a few minutes ago that you are given the floor, but, frankly, I thought that you are going to tell us something which is relevant to our proceedings here, which is relevant to your case. Frankly, I am not interested to listen to various nice thoughts about Naziism, et cetera, and I really do not understand what is your -- and Carla Del Ponte and Florence Hartmann. We are not here to talk about it, these rambling speeches about everything. Please save us from that situation, that we have to listen to you, and subject matters which have nothing to do with our work here. And I believe that you have to understand this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Judge Prandler, but you have to understand me too. In Carla Del Ponte's book, she says that the Croats are sons of bitches, corrupt sons of bitches. I've asked 50 bodies, the UN and others, whether I'm a son of a bitch and whether, given such a racist position, whether the indictment was drafted on the basis of such a racist position. That's what I asked, no one answered that question of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to join with Judge Prandler in objecting with this, and if we're going to allow speeches to be made, then the Prosecution will have a speech in response. This is inappropriate. That was a times for a motions to challenge the form and nature of the indictment. If there was any basis to believe that the indictment was invalid or improperly motivated, those motions would have, I'm sure, been filed and adjudicated at the proper time. We're way beyond that. Counsel will remember there are all sorts of things, jurisdictional motions, form of the indictment, amending certain paragraphs. We're way beyond that, now that's what Mr. Praljak wants to talk about. And if we're going to have speeches, then we'll have speeches by everyone. So I'll get up and talk about my views as well, if that's what the Chamber is going to allow. I fully endorse Judge Prandler's comments. This is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the decision was made by the majority. Judge Prandler and myself, we were in favour of letting you explain very precisely why you would no longer attend the proceedings. That's what we're interested in. The book written by Ms. Carla Del Ponte, I haven't read it. I saw one page, I'm telling you, but I didn't find it necessary to invest a few Euros in the purchase of that book. So leave the book aside, please, and do explain why, from an objective point of view, you no longer want to attend the proceedings. That's what we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll be briefer, in that case. I'm quoting what you said, Judge Antonetti. You didn't agree with the two of the Judges, and you read the following, I quote: "I believe that excluding documents of this kind is tantamount to a biased approach to the conflict." I'm claiming that each and every decision of scientific principle, each and every legal decision, must be publicly verified. It's a matter of publicly verifying the results obtained through scientific means and on the basis of the available facts. I am saying that we all, and that includes the Judges, arrive at logical conclusions, and we follow a methodology in accordance with our own knowledge or ignorance, in accordance with analytical minds. Our conclusions also depend on our physical and mental capacities, and so on and so forth. But in no science, not at any cost, is it permissible to ignore and exclude certain facts or premises that might challenge our conclusion, the information we have, or the judgement that we hand down. Therefore, I, in a fairly peaceful manner, can accept the fact that the Judges may have committed an error when deciding on my guilt, because it's a faulty interpretation. There is a faulty interpretation -- or a faulty interpretation is in-built in each person, it's a possibility -- as a possibility. However, I cannot accept, nor can Judge Antonetti accept, the exclusion -- the dismissal of facts that might serve to challenge the conclusion or the punishment that has been meted out, the judgement. As a result, in my opinion, there are several levels, legal levels, from main supreme constitutional courts. In this Tribunal, we have two levels. So in this case, certain sub-systems are being dismissed. There are no Serbs, there are no Mujahedin in this case, all the problems that concern refugees, expelled persons, all these problems have been excluded. Issues that concern the idea of a civil war have been excluded. The idea of a religious war introduced by the Mujahedin has been excluded, and all this is because of the tu quoque principle. And, finally why did Judges Trechsel and Prandler dismiss certain evidence? Do Judges Trechsel and Prandler want to reduce the system to a measure of their own understanding, to the framework of their own understanding, or are they reducing the system to what can be proved in advance, to a conclusion that can be proved in advance? Wouldn't it be fairer, more just, to abandon all the evidence in the case and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Praljak. I must protest here. You are speculating without real foundation on what my colleague and I, myself, are thinking. You are completely wrong, and I must state this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that I am wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I also would like to ad that here when you mention that we, in our understanding, we are using the system and we are against you. What would you like to prove? We are at an international court. Certain rules should be really respected and to be kept. I really believe that what you are saying, it is already too much, and although I am a person who can go along with many explanations, and I am, of course, careful not to be against anybody here, but, on the other hand, I cannot tolerate something which is being advanced against me and against my fellow Judges. So please try to be correct, and try to understand that you are -- really, what you are doing, it is counter-productive and you harm yourself. I have to tell you this frankly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why would I inflict damage on myself, act against myself, Judge Prandler, so that you are insulted, so that you are angry with me, so that you don't arrive at a certain judgement? You are professional judges, but on 50 occasions you are incapable of agreeing on certain elementary matters. So that is why I'm asking you whether it would be better to abandon evidence and to make it possible to arrive at a different conclusion from the one that you might arrive. In what way am I insulting you or the International Tribunal? You have dismissed evidence, and you haven't made it possible to follow scientific procedure that would enable one to reach a conclusion different from the one that you might reach. Why should one be insulted. Is it just because you are sitting there as a Judge, sitting at the Bench? Should I deify you as a result? No, I have a lot of respect for you. But on one occasion, Judge Prandler, I said that if someone should jump into the water, well, then it would be Praljak, but this is a rational issue I'm dealing with. I have 155 witnesses I wanted to call, and you have prevented me from doing that. I'm accelerating. You select evidence. Someone might, for example, dismiss all evidence on the nature of photons, but leave evidence on the nature of other phenomena, so other scientists may just come to the conclusion that there is only a matter of particle physics, certain things of that kind. I won't accept errors as a result of dismissing evidence, as a result of reducing the problem, because in the future other court bodies won't be able to check the method that was used to reach the judgement. This won't be possible in the future, and I won't accept that you prevent this from happening. When you reach your conclusions, you may say that this evidence has no value, but we are not gods, so perhaps one might, on a scientific and legal basis, come to other conclusions. So why should such a claim insult anyone? We're just discussing methodology here, and, therefore, I am trying to present the facts through 155 witnesses. I'm participating in the proceedings, but evidence is being dismissed, and I don't see why the picture should be distorted in this way. The very premises, not just the conclusion, but the very premises are being distorted, so I don't see why my human dignity should be trampled on as a result. I'll be guilty, if that is what is proven, but, Your Honours, the professional code of conduct states that all the elements have to be available so that your conclusion could be overturned in the future, if that is a possibility. There might be other courts. I might end up in the Court for Human Rights in Strasbourg if I become a member of the European Union. While I'm still alive, I have the right to attempt to prove my innocence. And if you bear in mind what has been said, for example, by Carla Del Ponte, well, I have the right to prove whether I'm guilty or not. If you read the 155 statements I have, and I spent a lot of money on them - it wasn't the Court's money - if you read that you will see that if anyone were to give his arm for you and to cure you, Praljak would do so. I don't even want to discuss the matter of mens rea. How are we going to measure mens rea? Well, it's necessary to see what a man is in a given moment, what he has done at a given time, in a given situation. How did he act, what did he do? Thank you very much. You'll receive a more detailed presentation of my arguments in writing in English. I have a normal -- I can no longer participate in this, but you can bring a judgement such as you see fit. If I participate in this procedure, it means that I'm accepting certain things, but throughout my life I have refused to accept certain things. When certain elementary or scientific procedure is no longer followed, I'm not in a position to accept such a situation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are not going to comment. You say that you are going to send us something in writing. We will read that document. That is all that I can say right now. We have another 12 minutes before we come to an end. We have the Defence counsel of Mr. Coric that should start cross-examination. Do you want to start tomorrow or do you want to make use of those 12 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it would be better if we started tomorrow. By the time we distribute the documents, two or three minutes will elapse, and it may be better for things to settle down and for all of us to calm down, and so I can start tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Something more technical. In the decision made by the Trial Chamber, the 92 bis, I was told that there was a mistake in the English translation and that a correction had to be made in the disposition. It wasn't said that the claim had been dismissed, but that it had been -- I don't know what it was based on, but there was a mistake in the English translation. Now, the Trial Chamber's legal expert tells me that the correction has been made this afternoon. So this has been postponed. It hasn't been rejected. It's just been postponed. It hasn't been dismissed. In the Defence teams and in the Office of the Prosecutor, there are no French speakers, unfortunately, that could explain the meaning of the words of the decisions that we are making. Sometimes that could allow us to avoid misinterpretations. But the correction has been made in the course of the afternoon. This is what I wanted to tell you. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. The Defence counsel for Mr. Coric will have one hour and ten minutes. If I'm not mistaken, that's 70 minutes. If we do not waste any time, we will hear the Defence counsel for Mr. Prlic, and then we will continue with the cross-examination by the Prosecutor, and we will make a decision on the other time allowed for the Prosecutor tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.51 p.m.,
